title: Pi Coding Agent Observability: HTML Specs with Gemini 3.5 Flash and GPT Image 2
summary: Dan answers a practical question - should agent specs be markdown, HTML, or HTML with images - by measuring instead of guessing. He runs three identical planning/build tasks through three Gemini 3.5 Flash agents using the Pi coding agent harness, streaming every event into his Pi agent observability dashboard (central server plus DB plus UI with swim lane, single-lane, and race views). Alongside the engineering agents he demos a product-focused 'Steel Man' agent that argues the bear case against an investment thesis (Apple as an AI distribution winner), generating UI components and citing 40 tool-called references. The surprise result: the markdown agent burned more tokens (170 events) than the HTML agent (100 events), proving you cannot know spec economics without observing them. He then shows the enhanced 'V spec' - markdown or HTML plans with images generated by GPT Image 2 - which his build prompt forces agents to read, and declares that all his plans are now visual specs. He connects the exercise to tokenomics (use tokens, generate value, arbitrage value) and previews evals as the next step after observability.
what_you_learn: You learn how to build a minimal agent observability pipeline (stream events to a server, store in a DB, render in a UI) and use it to compare spec formats and models on the performance-speed-cost tradeoff triangle. It also teaches the emerging practice of multimodal 'V specs' - plans with embedded images - and why measuring beats vibe coding when choosing how to prompt agents.

learnings.title: The question: markdown, HTML, or image-enhanced specs - and measuring beats guessing
learnings.detail: Prompted by Anthropic's 'unreasonable effectiveness of HTML' post and OpenAI's near-perfect image model, Dan frames the real question as the tradeoff triangle of performance, speed, and cost. He runs three Gemini 3.5 Flash Pi coding agents on the exact same prompt with three spec types: classic markdown, HTML, and an enhanced HTML 'V spec' with embedded images. Every event, turn, and tool call is captured in the Pi observability dashboard. His rule: more useful tokens outperform fewer useful tokens - the keyword is useful.

learnings.title: The observability architecture: stream events, store in DB, render in UI
learnings.detail: The system is deliberately simple: a centralized server that agents stream events to, a database so sessions survive refresh, and a UI that reads those events. The engineer intakes the information and closes the loop by improving the agents. Views include a compressed function mode, a visual form mode, a single-lane view for one agent's full trace, and a race mode that lays multiple agents' turns side by side for comparison. Observability matters even more for out-of-the-loop product agents than for terminal engineering agents.

learnings.title: The Steel Man product agent: an anti-sycophancy bear thesis machine
learnings.detail: Dan demonstrates a product-focused agent that steel-mans the opposite of your thesis: given 'Apple is an unappreciated AI distribution winner', it researches and argues the bear case with generative UI components (quote, catalyst timeline, valuation gauge). This counter-positional design fights agent sycophancy - models by default tell you what you want to hear. The agent did real tool-called research with 40 cited references, e.g. showing Mac mini is under 2% of Apple's revenue, and emitted a live artifact (a pie chart) during the run.

learnings.title: Inspect the start event: your real system prompt is bigger than you think
learnings.detail: Clicking into an agent's start event reveals the fully templated system prompt, session file and ID, and every loaded tool. Dan shows that stacking Pi coding agent extensions (communication tools, sub-agent delegation, session digging, skills) bloats the system prompt significantly - a decent chunk of context is just listing skills. You only discover facts like this by observing; even the Pi coding agent's own prompt is surprisingly large. This is why he streams observability on every agent via a single Pi extension.

learnings.title: The surprise result: markdown used more tokens than HTML
learnings.detail: Comparing the markdown and HTML planning agents, markdown used 29 turns and about 170 events while HTML used 17 turns and about 100 events, at similar context usage - markdown cost more this run. The cause is unclear (variance, or the markdown agent doing more codebase research), which is exactly the point: without looking at what your agents do you will never know the economics of the prompts you write. The correct follow-up is to turn the comparison into an eval run repeatedly for average results - evals come after observability.

learnings.title: Gemini 3.5 Flash: near state of the art with cracked speed, but priced like a mid-tier
learnings.detail: Dan is impressed by Gemini 3.5 Flash's tokens-per-second and near-state-of-the-art performance, making its performance-speed-cost tradeoff excellent for product agents - though he notes its price came in higher than expected for a 'Flash' model. His lens is cost per intelligence, not cost per token: if a more expensive model delivers the intelligence you need, pay it; and if a cheaper model like DeepSeek V4 Pro still gets the results and makes the right tool calls, switch to it - especially at product scale where agents run thousands of times.

learnings.title: V specs: embed images in plans and force agents to read them
learnings.detail: The V spec is a markdown or HTML plan with images generated by GPT Image 2 embedded inline. The build prompt is updated to say 'if there are images inside the plan, you must read them'. Image tokens are especially valuable for multimodal models like Gemini 3.5 Flash, which tops multimodal benchmarks. Caveat his observability tool missed: generating the images themselves cost $1-3, so full costing must include image generation.

learnings.title: HTML specs shine as living prototypes inside the plan
learnings.detail: An HTML spec is the same markdown content in HTML, giving a more visual-rich portrayal of UI components - Dan's agent mocked out the quote, timeline, and valuation gauge components from it. Because HTML renders, you get demo proof-of-concepts for parts of the work embedded directly in the plan, even for backend, DevOps, or product work. He stays deliberately economical with tags rather than using every HTML feature, and notes text is often still enough - the point is choosing the format consciously per tradeoff.

learnings.title: All plans are now visual specs - and planning is one of the two agentic constraints
learnings.detail: Dan's conclusion: he now plans exclusively with V specs - images always, plus HTML or markdown referencing them - because seeing interfaces and images while planning is superior for both him and the agent. This attacks the planning constraint, one of the two constraints of agentic engineering (the other is reviewing). Whether a spec format is worth its tokens always comes back to whether you understand the tradeoff triangle for that specific prompt, workflow, or software factory.

learnings.title: Observability feeds tokenomics: use tokens, generate value, arbitrage value
learnings.detail: The video ties measurement to the tokenomics chain: step one is using more (useful) tokens, step two is generating value from them, step three is capturing that value as revenue. Running lots of agents is a great starting point but a terrible ending point - you need valuable agents and then capture the value. The Pi observability extension, plus other composable slices like the Pi flat agent-communication network, stack into a custom harness that makes the tokenomics of every run visible.

learnings.title: Where this is going: multimodal specs and model specialization
learnings.detail: Dan predicts specs will keep getting more multimodal - text, image, audio, video in plans - with Gemini positioned as the leader thanks to its multimodal training advantage. Model providers are specializing: OpenAI shipping strong engineering and image models, Gemini topping multimodal. His standing advice for any open-source codebase or tool, including his own Pi observability repo: treat it as an option - take it, adapt it with your agents, specialize it, and make it your own.

key_points: If you do not measure your agents, you cannot improve them - observability is step one, evals are step two.
Markdown spec vs HTML spec on identical prompts: markdown used 29 turns and 170 events, HTML 17 turns and 100 events - cheaper is not what you assume.
The Steel Man agent fights sycophancy by arguing the opposite of your thesis with tool-called research and 40 cited references.
The start event reveals your real templated system prompt - stacked skills and extensions silently bloat it.
V specs embed GPT Image 2 images in plans; the build prompt must force agents to actually read them.
Judge models on cost per intelligence, not cost per token - and switch to cheaper models when they still get the results.
HTML specs double as rendered prototypes inside the plan - proof-of-concepts for free.
Tokenomics is a chain: use tokens, generate value, capture the value - do not get stuck token maxing at the bottom.
The Pi observability extension is one composable slice of a custom harness - treat every codebase you find as an option to adapt.
